summary: Adds new cipher suites to Transport Layer Security (TLS) that use the SEED block cipher for bulk encryption. This lets TLS implementations choose SEED as an alternative cipher. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: This document adds six choices to the list of ciphers that a TLS connection can agree on. Each of them encrypts the data with SEED, a block cipher designed in South Korea and used there for banking and online payment. The six differ only in how the two sides agree on the secret key.

subtitle: Six TLS cipher suites that use the SEED block cipher, a Korean standard, for bulk encryption.

tldr.problem: TLS needed a way to negotiate SEED, a block cipher developed by the Korea Information Security Agency (KISA) and widely used in South Korea, as the bulk cipher for protecting data.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines six cipher suites that all use SEED in CBC mode with SHA-1 in an HMAC construction, and differ only in the certificate type and key exchange method.
tldr.outcome: TLS implementations can offer SEED as an alternative to other bulk ciphers. The RFC says the new suites are not believed to be less secure than the corresponding older ones. It has since been updated by RFC 8996 and RFC 10015.

facts.label: Mode and hash
facts.value: SEED in CBC mode, SHA-1 in an HMAC construction

today: RFC 4162 is a Proposed Standard published in September 2005 that adds SEED cipher suites to TLS. The unit metadata lists RFC 8996 and RFC 10015 as updating it, so it should be read together with those documents. The text itself says SEED is widely used in South Korea for electronic commerce and financial services operated on wired and wireless PKI.

sections.title: What This Document Adds
sections.content:
This document proposes the addition of new cipher suites to the Transport Layer Security (TLS) protocol, as specified in the first version of TLS, to support the SEED encryption algorithm as a bulk cipher algorithm.

The cipher suite is the single name a TLS client and server use to agree on how a connection is protected. In the names used here, the parts of the name state the key exchange algorithm, the bulk cipher and the hash function, so the six suites differ only in the first of those.
sections.plainLanguage: A TLS cipher suite is a single name that stands for three choices: how to agree a key, how to encrypt the data, and how to check it arrived intact. This document adds six new names, all of which use the same cipher and differ only in the first choice.

sections.title: The SEED Block Cipher
sections.content:
SEED is a symmetric encryption algorithm that was developed by the Korea Information Security Agency (KISA) and a group of experts, beginning in 1998. Its input and output block size is 128 bits and its key length is also 128 bits. SEED has the 16-round Feistel structure: a 128-bit input is divided into two 64-bit blocks, and the right 64-bit block is an input to the round function with a 64-bit subkey generated from the key scheduling.

SEED is easily implemented in various software and hardware, because it is designed to increase the efficiency of memory storage and the simplicity of generating keys without degrading the security of the algorithm. In particular, it can be effectively adopted in a computing environment that has restricted resources, such as mobile devices and smart cards.

SEED is a national industrial association standard of the Telecommunications Technology Association of South Korea, and it is widely used in South Korea for electronic commerce and financial services operated on wired and wireless PKI. The algorithm specification and its object identifiers are described in RFC 4009.
sections.plainLanguage: SEED encrypts 128 bits of data at a time with a 128-bit key, and runs 16 rounds of a Feistel structure, where each round mixes one half of the block into the other. It was designed to be small and quick enough to run on a smart card or a phone.

sections.title: The Six New Cipher Suites
sections.content:
The new cipher suites have the following definitions, each with its two-byte code point:

  • TLS_RSA_WITH_SEED_CBC_SHA, { 0x00, 0x96 }
  • TLS_DH_DSS_WITH_SEED_CBC_SHA, { 0x00, 0x97 }
  • TLS_DH_RSA_WITH_SEED_CBC_SHA, { 0x00, 0x98 }
  • TLS_DHE_DSS_WITH_SEED_CBC_SHA, { 0x00, 0x99 }
  • TLS_DHE_RSA_WITH_SEED_CBC_SHA, { 0x00, 0x9A }
  • TLS_DH_anon_WITH_SEED_CBC_SHA, { 0x00, 0x9B }

The code points run from 0x96 to 0x9B, and the name of each suite states its key exchange, its bulk cipher and its hash function: SEED in CBC mode, and SHA-1.
sections.plainLanguage: Each suite has a two-byte number that goes on the wire during the handshake. The numbers for these six are 0x96 through 0x9B.

sections.title: The Cipher and the Hash
sections.content:
All the cipher suites described here use SEED in cipher block chaining (CBC) mode as a bulk cipher algorithm. SEED is a 128-bit block cipher with a 128-bit key size.

All the cipher suites described here also use SHA-1 in an HMAC construction, as described in Section 5 of the TLS specification. HMAC is the construction that computes the message authentication code: a value computed from the record data and a secret key, which the receiving side recomputes to check that the record was not altered in transit.
sections.plainLanguage: Every one of the six suites encrypts the same way, with SEED running in CBC mode, and checks the records the same way, with a keyed hash built from SHA-1. The two halves of a TLS record therefore look identical whichever suite is chosen.

sections.title: The Key Exchange in Each Suite
sections.content:
The cipher suites defined here differ in the type of certificate and the key exchange method. They use the following options:

  • TLS_RSA_WITH_SEED_CBC_SHA: RSA
  • TLS_DH_DSS_WITH_SEED_CBC_SHA: DH_DSS
  • TLS_DH_RSA_WITH_SEED_CBC_SHA: DH_RSA
  • TLS_DHE_RSA_WITH_SEED_CBC_SHA: DHE_RSA
  • TLS_DHE_DSS_WITH_SEED_CBC_SHA: DHE_DSS
  • TLS_DH_anon_WITH_SEED_CBC_SHA: DH_anon

For the meanings of the terms RSA, DH_DSS, DH_RSA, DHE_DSS, DHE_RSA and DH_anon, the document points the reader to Sections 7.4.2 and 7.4.3 of the TLS specification.
sections.plainLanguage: Half of the suites use RSA to establish the key and half use Diffie-Hellman, in its fixed, ephemeral and anonymous forms. Choosing between the six is therefore a choice of key exchange method, not of encryption.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The document says it is not believed that the new cipher suites are less secure than the corresponding older ones, and that no security problem has been found on SEED. SEED is robust against known attacks, including differential cryptanalysis, linear cryptanalysis and related key attacks, and it has gone through wide public scrutiny. It has been evaluated and considered cryptographically secure by trustworthy organizations such as ISO/IEC JTC 1/SC 27 and the Japan CRYPTREC committees. SEED has been submitted to several other standardization bodies, such as ISO with ISO/IEC 18033-3 and the IETF S/MIME Mail Security protocol, and it is under consideration. For further security considerations, the reader is encouraged to read the SEED self evaluation report.

For other security considerations, the document refers the reader to the security of the corresponding older cipher suites described in the TLS specification and in the AES cipher suites for TLS.
sections.plainLanguage: The document reports that SEED has been examined for the usual attacks on block ciphers and has been reviewed by outside standards bodies, and that the six suites are not expected to be weaker than the older suites they sit beside.

items.title: Round function input
items.text: The right 64-bit block, with a 64-bit subkey from the key schedule.
